newsitem.title: USA: Blue chips extend post-election surge to second day.
newsitem.headline: Blue chips extend post-election surge to second day.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks roared back from early losses to set another record Thursday as the market extended its post-election rally into a second day.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended up 28.33 points at 6,206.04 after Wednesday's gain of 97 points.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks also set a record, gaining 3.06 points to 727.65, and the NYSE Composite rose 1.36 to a record 384.91.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,390 to 1,053 on heavy volume of 500 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The Dow index continued its spectacular rise as it closed for the first time above 6,200 just one day after cracking the 6,100 mark. Thursday's gains came amid strength in bonds and lingering post-election enthusiasm.

"Bonds came back from the death of the dollar and apparently there was a decent 30-year bond auction," said Dean Witter chief investment strategist Peter Canelo. "We may get to 6,500 before year end or sometime in the first quarter."
The market has been in a bullish mood since voters re-elected Democrat President Clinton and a Republican Congress on Tuesday.
"We're still recognising all the good things in the election," Canelo said. "There's better hopes of deficit reduction."
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond gained more than a full point and its yield slumped to 6.54 percent from 6.62 percent on Wednesday.
"With yields this low, it's absolutely not competitive. Stocks are by far the better bet," Canelo said.
The defeat of a California ballot measure that would have made it easier for investors to sue companies if their stocks dropped also boosted the mood of investors, analysts said.
Technology companies with volatile stocks have been a favourite target for class-action lawsuits.

Intel Corp. rose 3-1/4 to 122-1/8 after the company's forecast on Wednesday of sharp gains in its fourth-quarter revenues as well as gross profit margins due to strong demand for personal computer chips.

The dollar's woes hurt the stock market early in the session as the currency fell after one of Japan's most influential policy-makers, known in financial markets as "Mr. Yen," signalled that the dollar's recovery was about to end.

Analysts said the dollar's retreat fuelled concerns on Wall Street that the Group of Three -- Japan, Germany and the United States -- had waited until after the U.S. elections to hint that their consensus for a strong dollar was breaking down.
In late New York trading, the dollar settled at Japanese 111.90 yen and 1.5112 German marks, down from 113.95 yen and 1.5175 marks on Wednesday.
Raising hopes for a good Christmas shopping season was news that September consumer instalment credit fell $2.6 billion, at a 2.7 percent annual rate, the first decline in more than three years.
"The optimism expressed by most investors suggest a merry Christmas," said Charlie Crane, director of research at Spears Benzak Salomon & Farrell.
Technology stocks helped lead the market higher. International Business Machines rose 1/2 to 133-3/4 and Cisco Systems added 3-1/4 to 64-1/2.
Hewlett-Packard gained 2-3/4 to 48-1/8 after SoundView Financial raised its 1997 earnings estimates for the company.
Chips & Technologies surged 3-7/8 to 23-5/8. The company said its stock might be moving in sympathy with Intel's rise.
Among other issues, Lowe's Cos. lost 4 to 39-1/2 on an earnings warning for the upcoming fourth quarter.
Republic Industries rose 2-7/8 to 33-5/8 on its acquisition of Alamo Rent-A-Car for $625 million.
Fila Holdings surged 7-1/4 to 82-7/8 on sharply higher quarterly earnings.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 8.65 points to 1,254.14. The American Stock Exchange index was up 1.38 at 579.25.
The average NYSE share was up 14 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was a record 7,045.824 up 31.929 or 0.46 percent.
